title: Pickleball Court Dimensions and Pad Size
metaDescription: Pickleball court dimensions in feet: 20 x 44 ft lines, 7 ft kitchen, net heights and the 30 x 60 ft pad to pour. A planning guide for backyard courts in Canada.
h1: Pickleball court dimensions: lines, net height and the pad size to plan for
intro: Every measurement you need to lay out a backyard pickleball court, in feet, with the pad sizes that work in a Canadian yard.
answer: A pickleball court is 20 ft wide and 44 ft long, the same for singles and doubles. The non-volley zone, or kitchen, runs 7 ft back from the net on each side. The net is 36 in high at the posts and 34 in at centre. The recommended total playing area is 30 x 60 ft.

paragraphs: The lines are the same at every level of play. Singles and doubles share one court, so there is only one layout to learn.
Lines are 2 in wide. Court measurements are taken to the outside edge of the boundary lines.

head: Part of the court
Measurement
rows: 7 ft from the net, each side
10 ft x 15 ft, two per side

paragraphs: Each half of the court is 22 ft deep. The first 7 ft back from the net is the kitchen. The remaining 15 ft is split by a centreline into two service courts, each 10 ft wide and 15 ft deep. The centreline and kitchen lines are the same 2 in width as the boundary.
On a tile court the kitchen can be laid in its own tile colour, so the zone reads at a glance from anywhere on the court.

The net is 36 in high at the posts and drops to 34 in at centre. A portable net system sets both heights for you. Permanent posts need sleeves set in the concrete, so decide which you want before the pad is poured.
Nets and posts are not part of a court kit. Choose the system that suits how you use the yard.

sections.h2: How big should the pad be?
paragraphs: The court itself covers 880 sq ft, but players need room to move around it. The recommended total playing area is 30 x 60 ft. That leaves 5 ft beside each sideline and 8 ft behind each baseline.
The smallest pad worth building is about 28 x 52 ft. It leaves 4 ft of run-off on every side, which is enough for casual doubles. Go smaller and the baselines sit too close to the edge.
If you are pouring new concrete and the yard allows it, ask for 30 x 60 ft. Look up as well. Lobs need clear air, so check for branches and wires over the court.

sections.h2: Matching a kit to your pad
paragraphs: Two pickleball kits cover these footprints. The 52 x 28 ft kit is $9,600 and the 60 x 30 ft kit is $11,670. Both are kit prices before freight and tax.
Tiles are roughly one foot square, so a layout can be resized in steps of about a foot when a pad falls between sizes. Measure the flat, hard area first. Then pick the kit at or just under it.
Want a hoop as well? The 60 x 30 ft multi-game kit keeps the same pickleball court and adds a basketball half court at one end.

faqs.q: How big is a pickleball court in feet?
faqs.a: 20 ft wide by 44 ft long, for both singles and doubles. With the recommended run-off, the total playing area is 30 ft by 60 ft.

faqs.q: How much space do you need for a backyard pickleball court?
faqs.a: Plan for a flat pad of 30 x 60 ft if you have the room. About 28 x 52 ft is the smallest size that still leaves 4 ft of run-off on all sides.

faqs.q: How high is a pickleball net?
faqs.a: 36 in at the posts and 34 in at the centre.

faqs.q: Is a pickleball court the same size as a badminton court?
faqs.a: The outline is. A doubles badminton court is also 20 x 44 ft. The inner lines and the net height are different.

title: How to Install Court Tiles: DIY Steps
metaDescription: How to install interlocking court tiles on concrete or asphalt: prep the pad, snap a chalk line, lock tiles with a mallet and trim edges. DIY guide for Canada.
h1: How to install modular court tiles on a concrete or asphalt pad
intro: Laying a court kit is closer to assembling flooring than to construction. Here is the order to work in and the mistakes to avoid.
answer: To install court tiles, sweep the pad clean, snap a chalk line square to one edge and start in a corner. Follow the numbered plan, pressing each tile into the last and seating the locks with a rubber mallet. Trim around posts with a fine-tooth saw, leave a small expansion gap at the perimeter and add edge pieces last.

sections.h2: What you need before you start
paragraphs: A court kit goes down on a flat, hard base. Concrete is the first choice and sound asphalt works too. Grass, soil and loose gravel will not hold the surface flat.
You do not need trade experience. If you can follow a numbered drawing, you can build the court. Gather the tools below and check the plan against the pallet before the first tile goes down.
list: Stiff broom or leaf blower
Tape measure
Chalk line
Rubber mallet
Fine-tooth saw for cuts around posts
Gloves and knee pads
The numbered layout plan from your kit

sections.h2: Step by step: laying the tiles
paragraphs: Work through the steps in order and do not skip the chalk line. A court that starts square stays square.
list: Step 1: Sweep the pad. Clear grit, twigs and anything else that would hold a tile off the surface.
Step 2: Measure the pad and mark where the court will sit, allowing for the expansion gap shown on your plan.
Step 3: Snap a chalk line along one long edge, then a second line square to it. These are your guides.
Step 4: Start in the corner the plan names. Set the first tile exactly on both chalk lines.
Step 5: Follow the numbered plan row by row, pressing each tile into its neighbour by hand.
Step 6: Seat every lock with a rubber mallet. A tile that sits proud is not locked.
Step 7: Check against the chalk line every few rows and correct any drift before it grows.
Step 8: Trim tiles around hoop poles and net posts with a fine-tooth saw.
Step 9: Keep the expansion gap clear at the perimeter and beside any wall, curb or post.
Step 10: Add the edge pieces last. Then walk the court and tap down anything that feels loose.

paragraphs: Hoop poles, net posts and drain covers are where the cuts happen. Hold the tile in position, mark it, lift it out and cut along the mark with a fine-tooth saw.
Leave a small gap around every post, the same as at the perimeter, so the surface can move without binding.
Plastic tile grows a little in summer heat and shrinks in winter cold. A court jammed tight against a curb, wall or post has nowhere to go and can lift. The gap on your plan gives it room.
The surface floats on the pad. Nothing is glued or fastened to the concrete. That is also why sections can be unlocked and lifted later to reach the base, move the court or extend it.
Plan an afternoon for a basketball half court with two or three people. A pickleball or multi-game court takes about a day. Tennis and full-court basketball kits are weekend jobs for a larger crew.
Pick a dry day. Stage the pallet contents beside the pad in plan order so nobody has to hunt for the next section.

faqs.q: Can I install court tiles myself?
faqs.a: Yes. The tiles snap together by hand and a rubber mallet seats the locks. Each kit comes with a numbered plan that shows where every section goes.

faqs.q: Do court tiles need to be glued down?
faqs.a: No. The tiles lock to each other and float on the pad. Nothing is glued or fastened to the base.

faqs.q: Can you lay court tiles on asphalt?
faqs.a: Yes, if the asphalt is firm and fairly flat. Fill wide cracks and level raised edges first.

faqs.q: What tools do I need to install court tiles?
faqs.a: A broom, tape measure, chalk line and rubber mallet cover most of the job. Add a fine-tooth saw if there are posts to cut around.

title: Concrete Pad for a Court: What to Ask For
metaDescription: Planning a concrete pad for a backyard court in Canada? What size to pour, the finish and slope to ask for, control joints, and when an old slab will do.
h1: How to brief a concrete contractor for a backyard court pad
intro: The tile surface is the easy part. The pad underneath decides how the court plays, so it pays to hand your contractor a clear brief.
answer: For a tile court, ask for a concrete pad the size of your kit plus a small margin, with a flat broom finish and a gentle slope of about 1 percent in one direction for drainage. Have control joints cut as usual, and follow your contractor's guidance on cure time before laying tiles.

sections.h2: Size the pad to the kit
paragraphs: Choose the kit first, then size the pad. A pad that matches the kit footprint plus a small margin on each side leaves room for the expansion gap and keeps the edge pieces fully supported.
Tiles are roughly one foot square, so a kit can be resized in steps of about a foot. If the yard forces an odd size, send the pad dimensions and the layout can be drawn to suit.
Ask for a flat, light broom finish. Tiles follow whatever is under them, so humps and dips in the slab turn into uneven bounce on the court.
Flat matters more than pretty. The concrete will be covered, so there is no need to pay for a decorative finish.

A court pad should be flat but not dead level. Ask for a gentle slope of about 1 percent in a single plane so water runs off one side. On a 30 ft wide pad that is a little under 4 in of fall across the width.

Open-grid tiles let rain pass through to the concrete, so the water still needs somewhere to go. Slope the pad away from the house and toward lawn or a drain. Avoid a crown down the middle. A single plane plays truer.
Concrete cracks, and control joints tell it where. Your contractor will cut or tool them at a spacing that suits the slab. The tiles bridge straight over them.
Tell the contractor about anything that goes in the ground before the pour. An in-ground hoop needs its own footing. Permanent net posts need sleeves. Mark both from your court drawing.

Slab thickness, base preparation and reinforcement depend on your soil and frost conditions. Leave those calls to the contractor, and check setbacks and lot coverage with your local municipality before booking the pour.

sections.h2: Curing before the tiles go down
paragraphs: New concrete needs time to cure before it is covered or loaded. Follow your contractor's guidance on when the pad is ready. Keep vehicles and heavy loads off the slab until they say so. Use the wait to settle your tile colours and line layout, and sweep the pad clean before the first tile goes down.

sections.h2: When existing asphalt or an old slab is good enough
paragraphs: You may not need new concrete at all. A driveway, patio or old asphalt pad can carry a court if it is firm, fairly flat and sheds water. Walk it after rain and check these points.
list: Small cracks with both sides at the same height are fine
Raised edges should be ground down
Dips that hold water should be filled
Soft, crumbling or heaved areas need repair before any tile goes on

faqs.q: How thick should a concrete pad be for a backyard court?
faqs.a: That depends on your soil, frost and what else will use the slab, so it is a question for your concrete contractor. The tiles only need the surface to be flat and hard.

faqs.q: Does a court pad need to be perfectly level?
faqs.a: No. It should be flat, with a slope of about 1 percent so water drains off.

faqs.q: Can I put court tiles on an old concrete slab?
faqs.a: Yes, if the slab is sound and fairly flat. Grind raised edges and fill dips first.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to pour a concrete pad in my backyard?
faqs.a: Rules differ from place to place. Check with your local municipality before you book the pour.

title: Court Kit Prices in Canada: Full Price List
metaDescription: Court kit prices in Canada for basketball, pickleball, multi-game, tennis and shuffleboard, with size, square feet and price per square foot for every kit.
h1: Court kit prices in Canada: every kit, size and price per square foot
intro: Every kit price on one page, with the square footage and the price per square foot worked out so you can compare sizes.
answer: Court kit prices run from $3,285 for a 42 x 6 ft shuffleboard lane to $44,050 for a 120 x 60 ft tennis court. Basketball, pickleball, multi-game and tennis kits work out to between $6.12 and $6.90 per square foot. These are kit prices before freight and tax, which are added to your quote.

paragraphs: Half court kits are listed width by depth and full court kits length by width. Every figure on this page is a kit price in Canadian dollars before freight and tax.
Half court kits sit between $6.65 and $6.90 per square foot. Full court kits run from $6.21 to $6.40.
Both kits carry the regulation 20 x 44 ft court. The larger kit adds run-off around it: 5 ft beside each sideline and 8 ft behind each baseline.
Multi-game kits put a pickleball court and a basketball half court on one 30 ft wide pad, in two line colours. The 60 x 30 ft multi-game kit is the same kit price as the 60 x 30 ft pickleball kit.
Tennis kits cover the largest footprints and carry the lowest price per square foot on this page. Both include the full 78 x 36 ft doubles court.
Shuffleboard kits are quoted in a flat-top tile so the discs can glide. That is a different tile from the other sports, so do not compare the per square foot figures across the two.

sections.h2: What the price includes and what gets added
paragraphs: A kit is the complete playing surface for the footprint listed.

Freight on a pallet of tile changes with distance and delivery access. It is quoted to your postal code and is not built into the list price. Tax depends on your province. Your quote brings kit, freight and tax together as one delivered number.
Custom sizes are priced on request.
list: Included: interlocking sport tiles for the full footprint
Included: edge pieces
Included: game lines for your sport
Included: a numbered layout plan
Not included: the concrete or asphalt base
Not included: hoops, nets and posts
Not included: lighting and fencing
Added to your quote: freight to your postal code
Added to your quote: sales tax

faqs.q: How much does a backyard basketball court kit cost in Canada?
faqs.a: Half court kits run from $3,420 for 25 x 20 ft to $9,970 for 50 x 30 ft. The 30 x 25 ft kit is $5,160. These are kit prices before freight and tax.

faqs.q: What does a court kit cost per square foot?
faqs.a: Between $6.12 and $6.90 for basketball, pickleball, multi-game and tennis kits, before freight and tax. Shuffleboard kits use a flat-top tile and run from $11.63 to $13.04.

faqs.q: Is shipping included in the kit price?
faqs.a: No. Freight is quoted to your postal code and added to the kit price, along with tax.

title: Multi-Sport Backyard Court Layouts
metaDescription: Multi-sport court layouts for Canada: how basketball, pickleball, badminton, volleyball and four square share one pad, and which pad sizes fit each combination.
h1: Multi-sport court layouts: how several games share one pad
intro: One flat pad can carry a hoop, a pickleball court and more. The trick is knowing which lines overlap cleanly and how much pad each game needs.
answer: A multi-sport court layers the lines for several games on one tile pad, using a second line colour so each game stays readable. A 60 x 30 ft pad fits a regulation pickleball court, a badminton court on the same outline and a basketball half court at one end. Volleyball needs 59 x 29 ft 6 in.

sections.h2: The court sizes you are working with
paragraphs: Start with the footprint of each game. Pickleball and badminton are the easy pair because their outer lines are identical.

head: Game
Court size
Planning note
rows: Takes nearly all of a 60 x 30 ft pad
Key 12 ft wide, free-throw line 15 ft from the backboard

paragraphs: On the multi-game kits, basketball lines are white and pickleball lines go down in a contrasting colour. Players follow the colour of the game they are playing and tune out the rest. The kitchen gets its own tile colour.

Two colours is a sensible limit. To add a third game, reuse lines where courts overlap. Badminton shares the pickleball rectangle, so only its inner lines are extra. Four square is a small box that can sit in a corner.

sections.h2: Which pad sizes fit which games
paragraphs: Volleyball is the tight one. On a 60 x 30 ft pad the court leaves about 6 in at each end and 3 in at each side. That is fine for casual games where players can step onto lawn. For real run-off, plan a bigger pad.

head: Pad size
Games that fit
rows: Basketball half court, pickleball with 3 ft behind each baseline, badminton
Basketball half court, pickleball at the recommended footprint, badminton, volleyball edge to edge
Full-court basketball, pickleball, badminton, volleyball with about 3 ft of run-off
Full-court basketball, volleyball with room around it, more than one pickleball court

sections.h2: Where the hoop and nets go
paragraphs: The basketball hoop sits behind the baseline at one end of the pad. The pickleball court runs down the length of the pad, so its net crosses the middle. A portable net rolls aside when the game changes. The hoop stays put.
For volleyball or badminton, plan on posts or a portable net system that adjusts in height. Hoops, nets and posts are not part of a kit, so pick the equipment before the layout is drawn.

Two multi-game kits come ready-made. The 50 x 30 ft kit is $9,890 and the 60 x 30 ft kit is $11,670. Both are kit prices before freight and tax. Each carries a regulation pickleball court and a basketball half court with key, free-throw line and arc.

Extra games can be drawn into the layout before the kit is produced. Name them in your quote request and they will appear on your court drawing. Tiles are roughly one foot square, so either kit can be resized in steps of about a foot to match your pad.

faqs.q: Can you play pickleball on a basketball court?
faqs.a: Yes. A regulation 20 x 44 ft pickleball court fits on a pad of 50 x 30 ft or larger alongside a basketball half court. Its lines go down in a second colour.

faqs.q: What size pad do I need for basketball and pickleball together?
faqs.a: 50 x 30 ft is the smallest pad that takes both. 60 x 30 ft gives pickleball its recommended footprint and a deeper basketball end.

faqs.q: Are badminton and pickleball courts the same size?
faqs.a: The outer lines are. Both courts are 20 ft by 44 ft. The inner lines and the net heights differ.

faqs.q: How many games can go on one court?
faqs.a: Two line colours keep a court readable. Three or four games are workable when some of them share lines.

title: Resurface a Tennis Court With Tiles
metaDescription: How to resurface a cracked asphalt tennis court with modular tiles instead of repaving: base condition, crack repair, pickleball lines and crew size in Canada.
h1: Resurfacing a cracked tennis court with modular tiles instead of repaving
intro: A faded, cracked court does not always need a paving crew. If the base is still solid, tile can go over the top and give you new colour, new lines and room for pickleball.
answer: You can resurface a cracked asphalt tennis court with modular tiles if the base is firm, fairly flat and drains. Fill wide cracks and level any heaves first, then lay the tiles over the top. A regulation 60 x 120 ft court is a weekend job for four or more people.

sections.h2: Tile over the top versus repaving
paragraphs: Repaving means removing or overlaying the asphalt, then coating and lining it again. It takes heavy equipment and a contractor. If the ground under the court is still moving, new cracks can follow the old ones.

Modular tile works differently. It floats on the existing surface and bridges small cracks, so the old asphalt stays out of sight under fresh colour and lines. You do the work yourself. Sections can be unlocked and lifted later if the base ever needs attention.

sections.h2: What condition the base must be in
paragraphs: Tile covers a tired surface. It does not fix a failed base. Walk the court after rain and check each of these.
If large areas have heaved or sunk, the base needs repair before any surface goes on. Photos of the court help when you ask for a quote.
list: Firm underfoot, with no soft or crumbling areas
Fairly flat, with no heaves or sunken sections
Water runs off and does not sit in large puddles
Cracks are stable, with both sides at the same height
Net post footings are solid if you plan to reuse them

paragraphs: Fill wide cracks so the tiles are supported across them. Grind or level raised edges and heaves. Fill dips that hold water. Pull weeds out of the cracks, then sweep or blow the whole court clean. Cut back overhanging branches and clear the fence line while you are at it, so leaf litter does not blow straight back onto the court.
The old surface does not have to look good. It has to be flat, hard and clean.
A 60 x 120 ft tennis pad divides into four quarters of 30 x 60 ft. That is the recommended total playing area for one pickleball court, so up to four pickleball courts fit.
Tennis lines go down in one colour and pickleball lines in a second. The tennis court stays regulation: 78 ft long, 36 ft wide for doubles and 27 ft wide for singles.
Two tennis kits carry the same doubles court. The difference is the run-off around it. Both figures are kit prices before freight and tax.
If your existing court is an odd size, the layout can be adjusted in steps of about a foot.
A regulation tennis kit covers 7,200 sq ft. Plan on a weekend with four or more people. Finish the base prep beforehand so the weekend is all tile.

Split the crew. Two people carry and place sections while two lock them down with rubber mallets and check the plan. Start from a chalk line snapped square to one edge, leave the expansion gap at the perimeter and fit the edge pieces last.

faqs.q: Can you put tiles over a cracked tennis court?
faqs.a: Yes, if the cracks are stable and the base is firm and fairly flat. Fill wide cracks and level heaves first.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to tile a tennis court than to repave it?
faqs.a: It depends on paving quotes in your area. The kit price is listed and you supply the labour. Get a paving quote and compare it with your delivered tile quote.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts fit on a tennis court?
faqs.a: Up to four on a full 60 x 120 ft pad. Each quarter is 30 x 60 ft, the recommended pickleball footprint.

faqs.q: How long does it take to tile a tennis court?
faqs.a: Plan on a weekend with four or more people once the base is prepped.
